ops.rationale: Takes the wording of citation report C1: the 50-year trends are tied to the Framingham Heart Study (n=9511, Schnabel_2015 abstract) instead of to the Wolf_1991 sample; the citation is kept.
ops.new_text: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common arrhythmia, and in people with asymptomatic AF the first presentation may be a stroke or heart failure \cite{Kashou_2021}. In the Framingham Study, AF was associated with a near fivefold excess of stroke. The stroke risk attributable to AF rose from 1.5\% at ages 50 to 59 to 23.5\% at ages 80 to 89 \cite{Wolf_1991}. Over 50 years of the Framingham Heart Study, the age-adjusted prevalence of AF rose about fourfold and its incidence more than tripled, in part through more intensive surveillance \cite{Schnabel_2015}. Identifying the people who will develop AF could therefore guide monitoring before a first complication. Clinical risk scores such as CHARGE-AF estimate this risk from routine variables \cite{Alonso_2013}. These scores need the abstraction of clinical data, which takes time, whereas a model applied to a single ECG at the point of care needs no additional data abstraction \cite{Kashou_2021}. The resting 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is thus a candidate source of risk information in its own right.

ops.rationale: Moves the survival design's fold sentences from 5.2 to the protocol paragraph of 4.2; per experiments/multihorizon.py lines 92 to 114 each test fold's risks come from models fitted on the other folds, and the penalised Cox model is fitted on the same training folds.
ops.new_text: The one-year comparison used stratified five-fold cross-validation at the patient level, repeated over five seeds, with each patient's scores averaged over seeds. The survival model used one stratified five-fold split, with an event within one year as the label for early stopping. Each patient's risk in the survival design came from the fold in which that patient was held out. The clinical Cox model was fitted on the same training folds as the networks. AUROC intervals come from 2,000 bootstrap resamples with percentile limits. At each horizon, cases had an event by the horizon and controls were AF-free beyond it, and patients censored earlier were excluded. Calibration and clinical use were assessed at one year in the survival sample, after two-fold cross-fitted logistic recalibration. They were measured by Brier scores, decision curves \cite{Vickers_2006} and operating points at the top 5, 10, 20 and 30\% of risk. Positive predictive value (PPV) and the number needed to monitor, its inverse, were recomputed at the proportion of cases among the cases and AF-free controls of the one-year design, 1,855 in 43,625. We report the study with reference to the TRIPOD+AI statement \cite{Collins_2024}, without a table of participant characteristics and without counts of missing values per clinical factor.

ops.rationale: States in the Results the comparison the Conclusion rests on: in table1_cis.csv the fused model's interval [0.7664, 0.7888] lies above ECG-only BTTN's [0.7275, 0.7517]; the CNN sentence is reworded so the ECG-only interval is given once.
ops.new_text: In the one-year design, the fused model had the highest AUROC of the methods compared, 0.7776 (95\% CI [0.7664, 0.7888]) (Table~\ref{tab:oneyear}). Its interval lay above the CNN's interval of [0.7226, 0.7469]. It also lay above the interval of ECG-only BTTN, 0.7397 [0.7275, 0.7517], so adding the clinical term raised the discrimination of the ECG term. It overlapped the interval of the clinical model, 0.7597 [0.7488, 0.7713], and the study reports no paired interval for this difference. The two estimates are therefore reported side by side. The CNN reached 0.7350, with an interval that overlapped that of ECG-only BTTN, so the two are comparable on this cohort. ECG-only BTTN exceeded linear BTTR, at 0.5967 [0.5824, 0.6115], with intervals that do not overlap.

ops.rationale: Removes the three method sentences that open the Results paragraph (moved to 4.2 by OP002, the three-network mean already in 3.2) and opens on the one sentence that the same risks were read at every horizon; the rest of the paragraph is unchanged.
ops.new_text: In the survival design, the same cross-validated risks were read at every horizon without refitting (Table~\ref{tab:horizons}). The fused model had an AUROC of 0.723 [0.701, 0.745] at 120 days, for onset in the 90 days after the blanking window, 31 to 120 days after the index ECG. Its AUROC was 0.727 [0.711, 0.743] at one year, 0.740 [0.727, 0.753] at two years and 0.745 [0.735, 0.755] at five years. The clinical Cox model had point estimates of 0.710, 0.711, 0.727 and 0.731, below those of the fused model at each horizon. ECG-only BTTN ranged from 0.658 to 0.676. The four horizons share the same risks and overlapping patients. They describe the behaviour of each model and are not independent replications. One reason for the lower one-year values of the survival design is its control group. At one year it includes patients who develop AF later, whereas the controls of the one-year design have no AF diagnosis.

ops.rationale: Replaces 'read from one survival model', which reads as one fit, by the cross-validated risks that 5.2 and the survival analysis (five folds, three networks per fold) describe.
ops.new_text: These results answer the research question within one health system. BTTN with the clinical term had the highest one-year discrimination of the methods compared. Its point estimates stayed above those of the clinical model at four horizons, read from the same cross-validated risks. Its ECG term alone was comparable to a CNN under the same protocol. After logistic recalibration within the survival sample, the predicted and observed one-year proportions of the fused model agreed closely in most risk deciles. It flagged more future cases than the clinical model at each flagged fraction. Per unit of energy, its ECG term responded most to the PR window of the beat. The gain of the fused model over the clinical model is small and consistent in direction. The one-year intervals overlap, and the study reports no interval of the difference that would establish it.

ops.rationale: Takes the wording of citation report C2: the McKeen_2025 abstract states the AF AUROC of 0.996 and the MIMIC-IV-ECG benchmark but not the data of that value, so the two facts are stated apart; the citation is kept.
ops.new_text: Published results give context for these values. On the hospital behind MIMIC-IV, a survival-loss CNN reached a C-index of 0.750 \cite{Sau_2026} and an image-based model 0.754 \cite{Zeidaabadi_2026}. A Montreal model reached an AUROC of 0.77 on external validation in MIMIC-IV, with a label source that its abstract does not state \cite{Jabbour_2024}. Elsewhere, an AUROC of 0.85 at one year \cite{Raghunath_2021} and a C-index of 0.781 over a short follow-up \cite{Riek_2026} were reported. These studies differ from the present one in horizon, outcome definition, sample and metric. A systematic review shows how far such choices move reported values \cite{Tsiartas_2025}. Identification studies \cite{Attia_2019,Yuan_2023} address another task. So does AF diagnosis from the ECG: a foundation model reported an AUROC of 0.996 for the AF label of multi-label ECG interpretation, and its authors released an open benchmark on MIMIC-IV-ECG \cite{McKeen_2025}.
